board_asks: identify an acid or a base with indicators (blue/red litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein, and olfactory indicators); write and balance the reactions of acids and bases - with metals (Salt + Hydrogen), with metal carbonates/hydrogencarbonates (Salt + Carbon dioxide + Water), acid-base neutralisation (Salt + Water), and metal-oxide / non-metal-oxide reactions; explain what happens to an acid or a base in water ($\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$/$\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$ ions) and why their solutions conduct electricity; use the pH scale (0-14) and its everyday importance (body pH, soil, digestion and antacids, tooth decay, acid rain); classify salts by family and by the pH of the salt; and give the preparation, properties and uses of the chlor-alkali products, washing soda, baking soda, bleaching powder and plaster of Paris (water of crystallisation). Most marks sit in writing the correct balanced reaction and in the pH reasoning.

big_idea.tagline: Sour or bitter - decoded by $\text{H}^+$, $\text{OH}^-$ and pH.
big_idea.body: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter and turn red litmus blue. In water an acid releases hydrogen ions, $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ (shown as the hydronium ion $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), and a base releases hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$ - and those ions explain everything else: why acid and base solutions conduct electricity, how they react with metals, carbonates and each other, and where a solution sits on the pH scale from 0 to 14. When an acid neutralises a base you get a salt plus water, and the chapter then follows one salt - common salt - as it becomes sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda, then closes with plaster of Paris (made from gypsum).

definitions.verbatim: Acid-base indicators are dyes or mixtures of dyes which are used to indicate the presence of acids and bases.
definitions.plain: Substances that signal whether something is acidic or basic by changing colour - litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are the common ones.

definitions.verbatim: There are some substances whose odour changes in acidic or basic media. These are called olfactory indicators.
definitions.plain: Indicators you smell rather than see - onion and clove oil lose their smell in one medium, so they can flag an acid or a base.

definitions.verbatim: The reaction between an acid and a base to give a salt and water is known as a neutralisation reaction.
definitions.plain: Acid and base cancel each other out, producing a salt and water: Acid + Base $\rightarrow$ Salt + Water.

definitions.verbatim: Bases which are soluble in water are called alkalis.
definitions.plain: A base that dissolves in water - like NaOH or KOH. All alkalis are bases, but not every base is an alkali.

definitions.verbatim: A scale for measuring hydrogen ion concentration in a solution, called pH scale has been developed.
definitions.plain: A 0-14 number line for how acidic or basic a solution is: 0 very acidic, 7 neutral, 14 very alkaline. The higher the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ concentration, the lower the pH.

definitions.verbatim: Acids that give rise to more H+ ions are said to be strong acids, and acids that give less H+ ions are said to be weak acids.
definitions.plain: Strength is about how fully an acid ionises, not how dilute it is - a strong acid produces more $\text{H}^+$ ions than a weak acid of the same concentration.

definitions.verbatim: Salts of a strong acid and a strong base are neutral with pH value of 7. On the other hand, salts of a strong acid and weak base are acidic with pH value less than 7 and those of a strong base and weak acid are basic in nature, with pH value more than 7.
definitions.plain: The salt inherits the stronger partner: strong+strong = neutral (7); strong acid + weak base = acidic (<7); strong base + weak acid = basic (>7).

definitions.verbatim: Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.
definitions.plain: The water locked into a crystal - $\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has five, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has ten; heating drives it off (blue copper sulphate turns white).

definitions.verbatim: Mixing an acid or base with water results in decrease in the concentration of ions (H3O+/OH–) per unit volume. Such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.
definitions.plain: Adding water lowers the ion concentration. Always add the acid to water slowly with stirring - the process is highly exothermic.

definitions.verbatim: Salts having the same positive or negative radicals are said to belong to a family.
The universal indicator shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions in a solution.
When pH of rain water is less than 5.6, it is called acid rain.
The process is called the chlor-alkali process because of the products formed– chlor for chlorine and alkali for sodium hydroxide.
Bleaching powder is produced by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime [Ca(OH)2].
Plaster of Paris is a white powder and on mixing with water, it changes to gypsum once again giving a hard solid mass.

concepts.title: Testing acids and bases with indicators
concepts.body: Indicators change colour (or odour) in acidic and basic media. Blue litmus turns red in an acid; red litmus turns blue in a base. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators (phenolphthalein is colourless in acid, pink in base), and substances whose smell changes - onion, vanilla and clove oil - are olfactory indicators.
concepts.tested: 1-2 mark: name an indicator and its colour change; identify three test tubes (acid / base / distilled water) using only red litmus paper.

concepts.title: Reactions of acids and bases
concepts.body: Acids react with metals to give a salt and hydrogen gas; with metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give a salt, carbon dioxide and water; and with bases in a neutralisation reaction to give a salt and water. Metal oxides are basic (they react with acids to give salt and water), while non-metal oxides are acidic (they react with bases).
concepts.tested: 3-5 mark: write and balance the reaction, name the salt and the gas, and describe the test for the gas evolved.

concepts.title: What all acids and all bases have in common
concepts.body: All acids produce hydrogen ions, $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ - shown as the hydronium ion $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ - but only in the presence of water; all bases produce hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$. These free ions carry current, so acid and base solutions conduct electricity, whereas glucose and alcohol contain hydrogen yet do not ionise and do not conduct.
concepts.tested: 2 mark: why dry HCl gas does not turn dry litmus red; why an aqueous acid conducts electricity while glucose solution does not.

concepts.title: Strength and the pH scale
concepts.body: Strength depends on how many $\text{H}^+$ (or $\text{OH}^-$) ions a solution produces, not on how concentrated it is - a strong acid ionises more fully than a weak acid at the same concentration. The universal indicator and the pH scale (0 very acidic, 7 neutral, 14 very alkaline) measure hydrogen-ion concentration: the higher the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ concentration, the lower the pH.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark: order solutions by pH / $\text{H}^+$ concentration; classify solutions as strong or weak, acidic or basic.

concepts.title: Importance of pH in everyday life
concepts.body: Living things survive in a narrow pH band (our body works around 7.0-7.8). Soil needs a suitable pH for healthy plants; the stomach uses hydrochloric acid for digestion, and antacids (mild bases such as milk of magnesia) neutralise excess acid; tooth decay begins when the mouth pH falls below 5.5; rain below pH 5.6 is acid rain. Bee and nettle stings are acidic and are soothed with a mild base like baking soda.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark: why antacids relieve indigestion; why tooth-cleaning is basic; acid rain / treating soil with lime.

concepts.title: Salts - family and pH
concepts.body: A salt is formed when an acid neutralises a base. Salts with the same positive or negative radical belong to one family (NaCl and $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ are sodium salts; NaCl and KCl are chloride salts). A salt of a strong acid and a strong base is neutral (pH 7); a strong-acid / weak-base salt is acidic (pH < 7); and a strong-base / weak-acid salt is basic (pH > 7).
concepts.tested: identify the acid and base a salt came from; predict whether the salt is acidic, basic or neutral.

concepts.title: Chemicals from common salt, and water of crystallisation
concepts.body: Common salt (NaCl) is the raw material for many chemicals. Electrolysis of brine - the chlor-alkali process - gives sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. Chlorine on dry slaked lime gives bleaching powder, $\text{Ca(ClO)}_2$. Baking soda ($\text{NaHCO}_3$) and washing soda ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$) are both made from common salt, and heating gypsum at 373 K gives plaster of Paris. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt ($\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$).
concepts.tested: 3-5 mark: uses of the chlor-alkali products; equations for baking soda, washing soda and plaster of Paris; what $10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ signifies.

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] Dilute sulphuric acid is added to zinc granules. Write the word equation and the balanced chemical equation, and name and test the gas evolved.

solution_steps.text: Zinc + dilute sulphuric acid $\rightarrow$ zinc sulphate + hydrogen.
The metal displaces hydrogen from the acid:
The gas is hydrogen; when a burning candle is brought near a hydrogen-filled soap bubble it burns with a pop sound.

examples.mark_logic: CBSE 3-mark: correct word equation (1) + balanced chemical equation with state symbols (1) + naming hydrogen and its pop-sound test (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] A metal compound A reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give effervescence; the gas evolved extinguishes a burning candle, and one of the products is calcium chloride. Identify A, write the balanced equation, and name the gas.

solution_steps.text: Effervescence with an acid and calcium chloride as a product means A is a carbonate - calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_3$.
The carbonate gives a salt, carbon dioxide and water:
The gas is carbon dioxide; it turns lime water milky and puts out a burning candle.

examples.mark_logic: CBSE 3-mark: identifying A as calcium carbonate (1) + the balanced equation with state symbols (1) + naming carbon dioxide with its lime-water / flame test (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] Dilute hydrochloric acid is added drop by drop to sodium hydroxide solution containing phenolphthalein. Write the balanced equation, classify the reaction, and give it in ionic form.

solution_steps.text: The pink colour fades as the base is neutralised:
Acid and base give a salt and water, so it is a neutralisation reaction; in ionic form the reacting ions are:

examples.mark_logic: CBSE 2-mark: the balanced molecular equation for NaCl (1) + naming it a neutralisation reaction and giving the ionic equation $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] 10 mL of a NaOH solution is exactly neutralised by 8 mL of a given HCl solution. What volume of the same HCl solution is needed to neutralise 20 mL of the same NaOH solution?

solution_steps.text: From the data, 10 mL NaOH needs 8 mL HCl, so the neutralising ratio of HCl to NaOH is fixed at 8 : 10.
The NaOH volume is doubled from 10 mL to 20 mL, so the HCl required also doubles.
So 20 mL of the NaOH solution needs 16 mL of the same HCl solution.

examples.mark_logic: CBSE 3-mark: writing the fixed HCl : NaOH neutralising ratio 8 : 10 (1) + scaling for the doubled NaOH volume (1) + the answer 16 mL with unit (1).

strategies.text: Reach for an indicator first - blue litmus red = acid, red litmus blue = base; phenolphthalein stays colourless in acid and turns pink in base.

Match the second reactant: metal $\rightarrow$ Salt + $\text{H}_2$; carbonate / hydrogencarbonate $\rightarrow$ Salt + $\text{CO}_2$ + Water; base $\rightarrow$ Salt + Water (neutralisation); metal oxide is basic, non-metal oxide is acidic. Then balance and add state symbols.
Hydrogen burns with a pop sound; carbon dioxide turns lime water milky and puts out a flame - name the gas by its test.
Lower pH means more $\text{H}^+$ and more acidic; exactly 7 is neutral. To compare two solutions, the one with the lower pH has the higher hydrogen-ion concentration.

Anchor each to NaCl: brine $\rightarrow$ $\text{NaOH} + \text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2$ (chlor-alkali); $\text{Cl}_2$ + dry slaked lime $\rightarrow$ bleaching powder; heat gypsum $\rightarrow$ plaster of Paris.

pitfalls.text: Thinking 'salt' means only sodium chloride. In chemistry a salt is any product of an acid neutralising a base - $\text{ZnSO}_4$, $\text{CaCl}_2$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ are all salts.
Forgetting that $\text{H}^+$ ions form only in water, so dry HCl gas does NOT turn dry litmus red - the separation of $\text{H}^+$ from the HCl molecule needs water.

Confusing strength with concentration. A strong acid ionises more fully than a weak acid at the same concentration; strong / weak is about the number of $\text{H}^+$ ions produced, not how dilute the solution is.
Adding water to a concentrated acid. Always add the acid to water slowly with stirring - dissolving an acid or base is highly exothermic and the mixture can splash out.

Mixing up baking soda and washing soda - baking soda is $\text{NaHCO}_3$ (sodium hydrogencarbonate) while washing soda is $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (hydrated sodium carbonate).
Writing plaster of Paris with a whole water molecule. It is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$ - two formula units share one water molecule.

formula_strip.label: Acid + Metal
formula_strip.tip: Test hydrogen: it burns with a "pop".

formula_strip.label: Carbonate / bicarbonate + Acid
formula_strip.math: Metal carbonate / hydrogencarbonate + Acid → Salt + Carbon dioxide + Water

formula_strip.label: Acids / bases in water
formula_strip.tip: An acid shows H⁺ only in water.

formula_strip.label: Baking / washing soda
formula_strip.tip: NaHCO₃ has no water of crystallisation; washing soda has 10.

formula_strip.label: Acid-Base Indicators
formula_strip.math: Litmus: acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue. Phenolphthalein turns pink with a base. Turmeric is another natural indicator.

formula_strip.label: Olfactory Indicators
formula_strip.math: Substances whose smell changes in acidic or basic solutions are olfactory indicators. Onion, vanilla essence and clove oil can be used as olfactory indicators.

formula_strip.label: pH of Common Substances
formula_strip.math: pH paper colours give a rough guide; neutral is 7, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. From the pH chart: gastric juice about 1.2; lemon juice about 2.2; pure water 7 (neutral); blood about 7.4; milk of magnesia 10; sodium hydroxide solution about 14. Rain with pH below 5.6 is acid rain; our body works within pH 7.0 to 7.8.

formula_strip.label: pH in Everyday Life
formula_strip.math: Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth falls below 5.5. Antacids neutralise excess acid in the stomach. Acid rain flowing into rivers lowers their pH and makes life difficult for aquatic organisms.

formula_strip.label: Dilution of Acids and Bases
formula_strip.math: Always add acid slowly to water with constant stirring; never add water to acid. Dissolving an acid or a base in water is highly exothermic.

formula_strip.label: pH of Salts
formula_strip.math: Salts of a strong acid and a strong base are neutral, with pH 7. Salts of a strong acid and a weak base are acidic (pH less than 7). Salts of a strong base and a weak acid are basic (pH more than 7).

formula_strip.label: Water of Crystallisation
formula_strip.math: Some crystals contain a fixed number of water molecules, called water of crystallisation: $\text{CuSO}_4\cdot5\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is blue and turns white on heating; moisten it and the blue returns. Washing soda is $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\cdot10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and gypsum is $\text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

formula_strip.label: Uses of Sodium Hydroxide, Bleaching Powder, Baking Soda, Washing Soda
formula_strip.math:
Sodium hydroxide (chlor-alkali process, Fig 2.8): de-greasing metals, soaps and detergents, paper making, artificial fibres.
Chlorine: water treatment, swimming pools, PVC, disinfectants, CFCs, pesticides. Hydrogen: fuels, margarine, ammonia for fertilisers.
Bleaching powder: bleaching cotton, linen, wood pulp and washed clothes; an oxidising agent in many chemical industries; makes drinking water free from germs.
Baking soda: baking powder (baking soda + tartaric acid) makes bread and cake rise; crispy pakoras in the kitchen; an ingredient in antacids; soda-acid fire extinguishers.
Washing soda: glass, soap and paper industries; making sodium compounds such as borax; a domestic cleaning agent; removing permanent hardness of water.

formula_strip.label: Strong and Weak Acids and Bases
formula_strip.math: The strength of an acid or base depends on the number of H⁺ or OH⁻ ions it gives. Acids that give more H⁺ ions are strong acids; those that give fewer are weak acids. The same idea holds for strong and weak bases.

shortcuts.text: pH < 7 acid, 7 neutral, > 7 base; lower pH = more H⁺.
Gas that turns lime water milky = CO₂; in an acid reaction, the other reactant is a carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.
Dilute acids by adding acid to water.
Salt of strong acid + strong base is neutral (NaCl, pH 7).
Burning matchstick near the gas: "pop" ⇒ hydrogen.
Dry HCl gas does not change dry litmus; acids show acidic behaviour only in water (H⁺(aq)).
Acid ne Neela ko Laal kiya; Base ne Laal ko Neela.

shortcuts.text: Baking soda mein Hydrogen, washing soda mein dus paani.
shortcuts.gloss: Formulae. baking soda NaHCO₃ (H, no crystal water); washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

shortcuts.text: Aadha paani wala POP, do paani wala Gypsum.
shortcuts.gloss: CaSO₄ hydrates. POP CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O.
Products of brine electrolysis. N = NaOH · C = Cl₂ · H = H₂ (order of the NCERT equation).
Salt types. strong acid + strong base → neutral salt.

third_tab_content.intro: For Chemistry the subject-adaptive third tab holds the chapter's key reactions - the formal core you must be able to reproduce, grouped by type. Every entry is a real NCERT Ch 2 reaction (word or balanced equation as the book gives it); the condition sits beside the arrow.

reactions.name: Acid + metal (general)
reactions.conditions: The metal displaces hydrogen from the acid as hydrogen gas

reactions.name: Base + metal (zinc + sodium hydroxide)
reactions.conditions: Warmed; sodium zincate forms and hydrogen is evolved (not all metals do this)

reactions.name: Carbon dioxide + lime water
reactions.conditions: Lime water turns milky (white precipitate of calcium carbonate)

reactions.name: Excess carbon dioxide + calcium carbonate
reactions.conditions: On passing excess $\text{CO}_2$ the milkiness disappears (soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate)

reactions.name: Metal oxide + acid (general)
reactions.conditions: Copper oxide + dilute HCl gives a blue-green copper(II) chloride solution; metal oxides are basic

reactions.name: Neutralisation - ionic form
reactions.conditions: All acids give $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ and all bases give $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$; Acid + Base $\rightarrow$ Salt + Water

reactions.name: Acid in water (ionisation of HCl)
reactions.conditions: $\text{H}^+$ ions separate from HCl only in the presence of water (hydronium ion)

reactions.name: Chlor-alkali process (electrolysis of brine)
reactions.conditions: Electricity through brine; $\text{Cl}_2$ at anode, $\text{H}_2$ at cathode, NaOH near the cathode

reactions.name: Bleaching powder
reactions.conditions: Action of chlorine on dry slaked lime; bleaching powder is $\text{Ca(ClO)}_2$

reactions.name: Baking soda (formation)
reactions.conditions: Sodium hydrogencarbonate made using common salt as a raw material

reactions.name: Baking soda on heating
reactions.conditions: On heating during cooking; the $\text{CO}_2$ released makes cakes soft and spongy

reactions.name: Washing soda (recrystallisation)
reactions.conditions: Sodium carbonate from heating baking soda is recrystallised to hydrated washing soda

reactions.name: Plaster of Paris + water $\rightarrow$ gypsum
reactions.conditions: Plaster of Paris sets to a hard mass of gypsum on mixing with water
